chunks: Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub narrated from Ibrahim ibn Hashim, from al-Nawfali, from al-Sakuni, from Ja'far, from his father, upon them be peace:

That Ali (peace be upon him) would detain a debtor in prison, then look into his case: if he had wealth, he would give it to the creditors; if he had no wealth, he would hand him over to the creditors, saying to them, 'Do with him as you wish: if you wish, hire him (as a laborer to pay off debt), and if you wish, employ him.' And he mentioned the hadith.

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: This report and the report of Talhah ibn Zayd do not contradict the report of Zurarah, which mentioned that he would not detain except the three whom he mentioned. Because that report implies two things: one is that he did not detain for punishment except those whom he mentioned; and the second aspect is that he did not detain them for a long time except those whom he excepted. Because detention for debt is only for the amount of time it takes for his situation to become clear. If he was destitute and that was known about him, he released him; and if he was not destitute, he obliged him to remain in it, as we clarified in what preceded.
ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic legal ruling on imprisoning a debtor who cannot immediately pay?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq details the practical application of debt detention, where creditors are granted authority over the debtor's labor if no assets exist, reflecting the Shia juristic view of debt as a right of the people. Shaykh al-Tusi’s commentary reconciles this with other reports by distinguishing between punitive detention and investigative custody, emphasizing that detention lasts only until the debtor's financial status is clarified. This underscores the principle of proportionality in Islamic judicial procedure, ensuring detention is not arbitrary but strictly tied to the debtor's ability to repay.
